text: You've now built tools the Chapter 2 way, wired straight into your own agent, and seen what an MCP server adds: the same tool definitions, discoverable and shareable across any MCP-compatible host. Neither approach is strictly better -- the skill is knowing which one fits.

Reach for a custom tool when it's specific to one application and will stay that way, when you need the tightest possible control over latency with no extra hop to a separate server process, or when you're prototyping and just need something working in minutes.

Reach for MCP when more than one AI application might want this integration -- building it once as a server avoids the M times N problem from Lesson 12 entirely. Check first whether a maintained server already exists, like the Filesystem Server or Sentry's own -- connecting is almost always less work than reimplementing it. MCP also supports users bringing whichever client they choose, without separate integration code per host.

Before building either one, ask three questions: will this ever be useful outside this one application, does a maintained server for it already exist, and are you prototyping or building infrastructure other people will depend on? A no, no, and prototype points back to Chapter 2. A yes to either of the first two points toward MCP.

You now have both tools in hand -- direct tool-calling for a genuinely one-off integration, and MCP for one worth standardizing and sharing. Chapter 4 moves on to agent architecture itself: ReAct, planning, multi-agent systems -- patterns that apply identically whichever way your tools got built.
